question: A patient receiving cyclophosphamide chemotherapy develops painless haematuria. Which toxicity-specific amelioration strategy should have been co-prescribed?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cyclophosphamide is metabolised to acrolein, which accumulates in bladder urothelium and causes haemorrhagic cystitis. Mesna is a uroprotectant that binds and inactivates acrolein in the urine. Concurrent IV hydration increases urine flow, reducing contact time.
Leucovorin rescue is used with high-dose methotrexate to prevent bone marrow and mucosal toxicity — not for cyclophosphamide-induced haemorrhagic cystitis.

answers.text: Amifostine (a free radical scavenger) given 30 minutes before each dose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Amifostine has cytoprotective properties and is used to reduce cisplatin nephrotoxicity and radiation-induced xerostomia, but Mesna is the specific and preferred agent for cyclophosphamide uroprotection.
Ondansetron prevents chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting — it has no role in preventing haemorrhagic cystitis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Toxicity Amelioration block. Cyclophosphamide → acrolein → haemorrhagic cystitis → prevented by Mesna + IV hydration.
Excellent. Mesna + hydration is the standard prophylaxis for cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide-induced haemorrhagic cystitis — one of the most high-yield toxicity amelioration pairings.
